body:
An unseen class is wasted budget or the whole point. The benchmark decides which, not the data.

Active learning picks what a human should label. When the pool contains classes the model has never seen, two literatures give opposite orders under near-identical names.

Open-set active learning counts every queried unknown as waste. Active category discovery treats unknowns as the reason to query at all. In this paper I read the two against each other.

The filtering camp's own results undercut its framing. Leading methods target a query precision of 0.6, which means about 40 percent of each query is unknown, and accuracy barely moves when that target varies.

What separates the camps is a price. In the one published sweep (MQ-Net's, not my experiment), confidence sampling scored 91.05 when an unknown query cost 0.5, tied with SIMILAR, a purity-first method. At a price of 4 it fell to 80.06 while CCAL held 87.25. Every benchmark I examined fixes that price at 1 and none measures it.

→ Say which held-out classes count as irrelevant.
→ Say what an answer about an unknown costs.
→ Don't compare the two objectives without both.

The full paper is attached below.
question: When you budget annotation, does a label on a class you didn't expect count as a cost or a find?
